title: Matthew 13:47–52
context: Jesus adds the dragnet parable of final separation, then asks whether the disciples understand and compares the trained kingdom scribe to a householder bringing out new and old treasure.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What earlier interpreters on each side wrote about Matthew 13:47–52.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Every scribe instructed unto the kingdom of heaven - That is, every duly prepared preacher of the Gospel has a treasure of Divine knowledge, out of which he is able to bring forth all sorts of instructions. The word treasure signifies any collection of things whatsoever, and the places where such collections are kept.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 13:47–52)

reformed.quote: The first two of these parables are intended to instruct believers to prefer the Kingdom of heaven to the whole world, and therefore to deny themselves and all the desires of the flesh, that nothing may prevent them from obtaining so valuable a possession. We are greatly in need of such a warning; for we are so captivated by the allurements of the world, that eternal life fades from our view; and in consequence of our carnality, the spiritual graces of God are far from being held by us in the estimation which they deserve.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 13:47–52)

verses.text: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a dragnet that was cast into the sea and gathered some fish of every kind,
verses.arminianNotes:
A net gathers fish of every kind. The kingdom’s catch is mixed in this age—broad gathering before sorting.

Cast the net widely. Grace invites many kinds into the hearing of the gospel while warning that gathering is not yet final approval.
verses.reformedNotes:
The net’s catch is indiscriminate in kind. Kingdom history includes a mixed haul until the shore.

God’s kingdom purpose includes present gathering that awaits eschatological sorting.

verses.text: which, when it was filled, fishermen drew up on the beach. They sat down and gathered the good into containers, but the bad they threw away.
verses.arminianNotes:
Fullness brings the shore, sitting, sorting—good kept, bad thrown away. Separation is careful and final for the catch.

Do not confuse being in the net with being kept. Grace calls for living faith that proves “good” in the Master’s sort.
verses.reformedNotes:
Timing (“when it was filled”) and sorting belong to the fishermen’s work at shore.

Fullness and separation are appointed. God will complete the catch’s evaluation.

verses.text: So it will be in the end of the world. The angels will come and separate the wicked from among the righteous,
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus applies the net: end of the age, angels separate evil from righteous. Final judgment is personal and moral, not merely institutional.

Repent and trust Christ now. Grace still distinguishes paths while the net is in the water.
verses.reformedNotes:
Angelic separation in the end of the world is certain. Evil and righteous will not remain mingled forever.

God’s agents execute His verdict. History bends toward that shoreline.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm angelic final separation. Arminians typically press present grace-enabled repentance before the sort; Reformed interpreters emphasize the certainty of God’s decreed end-of-age separation.

verses.text: and will cast them into the furnace of fire. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus repeats hard eschatology so hearers cannot shrug.

Classical Arminians keep the invitation open and the warning sharp: flee to Christ while grace calls.
verses.reformedNotes:
The repeated furnace line seals the net parable to the weeds explanation. Judgment language is Jesus’ own.

God’s justice will match the Son’s word—severe against unrepentant evil.

verses.text: Jesus said to them, “Have you understood all these things?” They answered him, “Yes, Lord.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus checks understanding; they answer “Yes.” Discipleship includes accountable comprehension, not endless fog.

Claim understanding only if you will live it. Grace enables true yes; empty assent is rocky-soil danger.
verses.reformedNotes:
Christ examines His own: Have you understood? Their yes becomes the hinge for the next image.

Understanding is gift and stewardship. The Teacher who gave parables also quizzes the heart.

verses.text: He said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been made a disciple in the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a householder, who brings out of his treasure new and old things.”
verses.arminianNotes:
A kingdom-trained scribe is like a householder bringing new and old from treasure. Torah and Jesus’ kingdom word belong together in wise stewardship.

Be trained, then share generously. Grace forms teachers who refuse both novelty-idolatry and dead traditionalism.
verses.reformedNotes:
Training for the kingdom produces a householder of treasure—new and old brought out under Christ.

Scripture’s fullness and the Messiah’s fulfillment are both wealth. God equips scribes for the church’s storehouse.
verses.keyContrast: Both honor trained kingdom teaching that holds new and old. Arminians stress grace-enabled responsible stewardship of the treasure; Reformed readers commonly highlight God’s training and provision of teachers for His house.
